lines.text: [indistinct audio — sound check]
Hello. [testing the mic] Hello. How are you? Hello. How's it going?
Hey. My name is David Choe. This is DVDASA. This is series four in a solo podcast. I'm here at the ranch. There's a third episode that I filmed and recorded, which — I don't know where it is.
It's missing. So here's number four. I may repeat some stuff, but who cares? I hate disclaimers, but this isn't a show for everybody, and you'll know quickly, right away, whether it's for you or not.

It's for a very specific person, and as soon as we start the show, you'll know right away if it's for you or not. I'm gonna give a lot of conflicting advice. And so — there's a lot, I gotta put a disclaimer, because there's a lot of idiots out there. [mock voice] Hey, he contradicted himself! [deadpan] Yeah, no shit.

I'm gonna say a lot of shit, and whatever I say to you, you pick what you want, get rid of what you don't want. And whatever I say to you that speaks to you at this moment in your life — currently, right now — take that. And then at other points, throw away whatever you don't need. Purging, constantly purging. [mock voice] You know, hey, you said that, and then you said this.

Yeah — because that was true for you today, and then ten years from now that won't be true. So that's why I say this is specific information for a specific person right now. So, not to alienate the audience, but um —

Happy to be here today. Beautiful outside, fresh air, all these windows. Let me start off by just saying, I went to a concert — our South African friends, Die Antwoord. Saw them in a show in LA yesterday, and I ran into, for the first time, Flea from the Red Hot Chili Peppers. Amazing. Beautiful, beautiful spirit. And we had just the —

— best conversation about creativity and art and music. And we just brought out super hard. I mean, here's a guy that's been in a band that's been called all kinds of stuff, to mainstream success, who raised a beautiful daughter, kids. You've seen him in Roadside Prophets or The Big Lebowski or any other movie he's been in, any project that he's in — he always gives it his all.

He goes 100%. And then you got Die Antwoord, the band. And people that know I'm friends with them, they go, [mock voice] hey, what is this? Is this a joke? No, this ain't a fucking joke! It's fucking serious!

It's serious as shit! And you know what? Once again with the contradictions — yeah, it is a joke. But guess what? It's a cosmic joke that we take so seriously. I feel like Flea, Die Antwoord, the shit I do — and there's tons of people out there —

We're cosmically tapped into this energy of a wolf with a dolphin head and angel wings that shoots rainbows out the back. And that might not make any sense to you, but we don't play by your rules — is what you don't understand.
You sit there and you criticize and you comment and you critique us and you hate on us, and you keep doing that. But we don't play by your rules. We don't even live in your reality.

We created our own. [mock whining] Oh, you sit there and you say, I want your life, I want your life, I want to do the shit you do — but you think someone just handed us the keys? We're world-building. We created this world. We create our own universe, our own reality, our own rules that we choose to break whenever we feel like it.

So if you feel like you're tapped into this energy, or you want to tap in — then this is the show for you. I'm gonna speak a little bit, and if I miss anything, then there's three, or two, other solo podcasts before this where I try to address everything.
I'm talking specifically about art, painting, creativity, and just how to live better. How to live your life in a good way.

So, where do I start? I mean, there's so many places. Let's see. I guess I'll just start with the title of our show — DVDASA. Double Vag, Double Anal, Sensitive Artists. And I'll address the sensitive-artist part, because the thing that inspires many, many songs, many paintings, is love — and the absence of love, and heartbreak. So I'll speak to that right —

— now, because there's a lot of people out there listening right now that are hurting. And so I'm going to speak specifically about cheating. I'm a very transparent person. I leave it all out. I'm not what you would call a mysterious artist. I talk literally every week for six hours about my shitting habits, so there's not anything I hide. I lay it all out there for you to see.

I'm very transparent. And so, you know, when you lay yourself out there in the open like that, you leave yourself open to be judged, and sometimes the limelight burns. So today I will speak of the hurt. And — [beat] that last part, which is a joke. Sorry, I'm gonna cut in and out, but —

When people ask me, is this a joke? Are you serious? Are you just fucking with us? It's like — yes, I am. And the way you do it successfully is to take the joke as serious as possible. To invest everything into this joke, into this surreal life, into this other reality. It's world-building. You're creating an entire alternate reality for yourself that you live in, where you —

— just end up not relating to the rest of humanity anyways. But the rest of humanity — fuck them, who gives a shit anyways. So today I'm going to speak right now not about art, not about any of this, but matters of the heart. I'm going to talk about cheating. So, when I lay it all out there —

People go, how did you get your start? How did you start? And I've told people: I did credit card fraud, forgery, shoplifting, robberies, whatever. I went to jail. I paid. I paid my dues for this. And this is a guilt that I still carry with me, and I try to make amends, and —

— try to do as much for society and the human race as I can, because I do still feel guilty. And I'm Korean, so I carry this guilt with me. But when people find out about that stuff — because you can never escape your past, those things always creep up — they go, this guy's a vandal, he does graffiti,

he has no respect for public property, he's a thief. All kinds — he's a womanizer. Like — you judge me. When I steal from a department store or graffiti a wall, I don't know who the victim is. I'm not saying that's okay, I'm not justifying it, but I don't know who these —

— people are. They're strangers. But when it comes to cheating — I mean, I've never cheated in my life. I've been in three serious relationships, and besides that, I've been single. I don't cheat. That's not what I do. And the close unit of friends that I've grown up with — none of the friends

that I grew up with cheat. They're good guys. But just living in this world, and traveling, and meeting a lot of people — old, young, all different walks of life — everybody cheats. We're fucking animals. We fuck everything. And so all these people judging me — oh, look at the kind of — you're all

despicable fucking pieces of shit. You all fucking cheat, and you sit there and you judge me. You're the ones committing the most heinous crime, because you're betraying not a stranger. You're not painting on the wall of a stranger. You're lying and cheating to someone who you look in the face and you say you love the most. That's the most heinous. And so I don't want to —

— do that. I don't want to lie to someone who I say I love and who's in my life. And so I've been single for ten years, and Critter's been single for about three or four years. We spend a lot of time together. And so me and Critter share similar things, and our number one thing

is: we don't like to hurt people. Like, I don't want to cheat. I love to fuck. And I'm going to speak for Critter right now — he loves to fuck. And so when you love to fuck, which we all do, the thing that happens is you end up cheating. You know, your options — you're on the road, who knows, social media, you meet someone, you see that someone from high school is single — so you end up cheating.

But it's horrible. It's heinous. I — I am sorry, I'm sitting here judging, but you're literally lying to — and then you always see them: [mock voice] oh, I can't believe he or she did this to me. You really — you can't believe it? You have a history of it. You've done it, other people have done it to you, you've seen that happen to your parents — and you really can't believe it?

That's just what people do. Besides like a handful of people, everyone I've ever met fucking cheats. They confide in me, and I go, oh, this is fucking disgusting. And so I tell everyone I'm single, because I'd rather be honest — which hurts them, when you tell them, I don't want to be with you because, you know, your pussy smells, or whatever the reason. However shallow, or whatever it is —

But it's because I say to them, it's because I don't want to hurt you. But let's get real — the title of the show, the last S-A, Sensitive Artists. When I say I don't want to hurt someone, when Critter says I don't want to hurt someone, the underlying truth in that is: we don't want to get hurt. Because to allow

ourselves to get hurt — then it hurts. And being hurt sucks. And nothing hurts more than emotional pain. Physical pain, you heal. The scar tissue, all that shit on your heart — that takes fucking forever. And once that shit keeps on happening, then you're numb to it. So all I gotta say to you — and I will definitely sound like a hypocrite right now —

— is: don't be scared. Don't be scared to love. Don't be scared to let your graffiti-covered walls down and let love in. Because when you let love in, what you're doing is letting yourself wide open to get hurt. But from getting hurt — and I don't mean to sound like a calculated person — enjoy the dance. As Pusha T says, enjoy the fucking dance. Did you enjoy the dance?

Nothing lasts forever. You don't know if it's gonna — you have one life. Enjoy your time here. Get hurt. Love. Fuck. Do everything. And when you get hurt, I'm telling you from experience: the hurt is such an intense emotion that the amount of creativity that's going to come from that is going to be unbelievable. It's going to be unbelievable. The pain — use it. Don't kill

yourself. Don't let it crush you. Take a few sad days to yourself, sulk — Sulkamania, sulk to yourself, whatever, go goth, listen to some Smiths or Cure or whatever — but don't let it destroy you. Use that pain, create with it. That's all I'm saying. We're all sensitive

out there. Critter's a big strong guy, he's sensitive. I'm an artist, I'm sensitive. Everyone's sensitive. So look — we're all sensitive artists. I'm just saying, don't be scared. Don't be scared. You've heard me say it here a million times. You heard it on the David Chang episode, you've heard me say it on the solo podcast, and I can't say it enough. Here I am on the fourth solo, and I'm gonna

say it again: comfort is the killer of creativity. A lot of you listening right now are in the comfort of — I don't know, your home, your office, you got your Beats headphones on, you're sitting in your mom's house, your dad's house, you got snacks, you got snacks, you're chilling, you're comfortable right now, you're laughing, you look at this fucking idiot

in this room just talking to himself. I don't give a shit. I'm in a room talking to myself, it's fucking a hundred degrees, I'm wearing a wig, my balls are sweating — I don't give a fuck. Okay? I choose this. I choose this, because I want to help you help me — help me — help me help you. Okay?

Comfort is the killer of creativity. You got it all right now — you got your PlayStation, you got your flat screen, you got mom doing your laundry, you got a nice place in a nice suburb, you got a nice — [shouting] YOU'RE A FUCKING ARTIST!

Be a fucking dangerous, badass, motherfucking artist! Okay? LIVE! What do you — [mock whining] oh, I just want to be comfortable. You have the whole rest of your life to be comfortable. Get out there!

Where do you live right now? I don't know where you live. Move to fucking Detroit, Baltimore, Chicago, New York, LA. Move to a big city — and not only that, move to the shittiest part of that city. Detroit — you can fucking buy a whole block for nothing. You don't even have to buy it, just go there, squat there. [mock whining] Oh, I'm scared. Well, then be scared.

Learn what it's like to be scared. Struggle. Fight. Fight — you're a fucking artist. You think anyone wants your shit? Chris Rock says: robbers don't steal books. They don't steal art. No one's gonna fucking break into your shithole squat house in Detroit and steal your art. It's not that good.

Especially not — to steal your shitty art. Your art's shitty as fuck. So just do it. Live. [mock whining] Oh, like, in New York City rent is so high and I don't have any space. Then go to Detroit and have the whole fucking 20,000-square-foot warehouse to yourself.
Yeah, it's going to smell like bum piss. Yeah, there's going to be bird dookie. Yeah, there's going to be homeless people wandering in there. But who gives a shit? What are you saving it for?
What are you saving it for? What are you waiting for? Once again, we go back to the movie Gattaca. Science fiction movie with Ethan Hawke and Jude Law. [imitating the brother] How did you do it?
When the superior brother asked the lower brother, who doesn't have the genetic superiority — how did you do it? How did you win in the swim? And he said, you know how I did it?

I didn't save anything for the swim back. And if you listen to the show, you've heard me say it a million times. I didn't save anything for the swim back. What is that? What does that even fucking mean?
We're all swimming. We're all swimming up a mountain. We're all swimming across the ocean.
What is it for? What are you saving it for? What is this comfort, this safety? Let's play this tape out to the end. Let's do it right now.

I just — what is this obsession with trying to be safe and have all these — don't you want to live? You know, I ran into Anthony Bourdain in New York City. I was on the fourth season of Thumbs Up, and I see him — my uncle Tony — and I say to him, I say: three days —
Three days into this show I had a breakdown. I was like, I don't even want to do this. I'm fucking rich, I'm a fucking successful artist. What am I doing on the side of the road begging for a ride?

And I wanted to call him — and here's Anthony Bourdain, who's been on the road exploring, showing you guys the fucking world, who puts himself through all this discomfort to show you, in the comfort of your own home, on television, on airplanes, in hotel rooms — and he said the same thing. He said, Dave, I just had a nervous breakdown myself,

and I was in the middle of shooting something and I just said, what the fuck am I doing? And I was like, oh, I'm glad I didn't call you, because that would have been crazy. And so I said, so then why do you do it? Why do you do it? And he goes, [imitating Bourdain] well, what am I gonna do, just sit at home and watch The Simpsons

and jerk off to porn? And I was like, that sounds pretty cool. But he's like, anyone can do that. He's like, that doesn't make for an interesting life. So you ask yourself right now: do you want an interesting life? Do you want to go out and meet interesting people and dance? Or do you want to

sit home and watch The Simpsons and jerk off, and call — let's wrap it up, let's call that a life. That's it, I did it. [mock voice] Oh, I can quote any line from Bart Simpson from any series of The Simpsons. It's like — really? That's what you care about? You've gotten too fat.

You've gotten too lazy. And I ask yourself — the safety, the society we live in with insurance and lawyers and wills and, I don't know, just protective gear and all this — like, I overanalyze things. So one of the things I do now in therapy with my therapist is we sit around, and I've made a lot of bad, bad choices in my life, which — because I did a jiu-jitsu move,

aikido move, and used the force of something negative and turned it into something positive — that's called secondary gains. That's like me going to jail and then having a sold-out art show of all the art that I made in jail. That's me taking a horrible situation and turning it into a good one.

Secondary gains. Can I get out of jail and just fucking tattoo my face and talk about how horrible it was and be a fucking loser? Of course. That's the easy choice. That's an easy choice. But that's jail — talk about uncomfortable, the most uncomfortable place you could ever be — and then to turn that around into something creative. So let's play the tape out. When

I say let's play the tape out — that's something that my therapist loves to say. It's like, any decision you want to make right now — you're at home, you saved your money, say you're married and you have a brand new baby. I don't know. I don't know what your situation is, I don't know

what our demographic is. I have no idea. I don't know if white people listen to the show, or Asians, or blacks, or whatever. But let's just say — let's just say you're not feeling it. You don't feel good, you're at a standstill in your life, everything's boring to you, the lust for life has left you, nothing interests you anymore. And you're like, should I take all the

money that I've worked my whole life working at this minimum-wage job, and invest in this dumb idea — I don't even know what it is — like a new kind of rubber band, that's like way superior in your mind to the old rubber band.

I just made that up. I have no idea what your fucking stupid invention is. But like I said from the beginning, we take a joke, and we take stupidity, and we fucking treat it with respect and put all of our energy and heart into it.

That's the difference between anyone else being like, huh, that's dumb. Yeah, look at Die Antwoord. It's easy to sit there and watch this band and go, oh, this is a joke band. But when you go see them live, you're like, this motherfucker has fucking Travis Bickle'd and just trained his body to become one with the music.

It's the greatest live show you can see today. And so when you're sitting there and I say, play the tape out — [mock whining] oh my god, the last ten years I've worked, enslaved, at this shitty office job where I hate the boss, and I've been treated like shit. Am I really, really ready to take all that money and

risk the well-being of my house, my newborn baby, and my wife on this crazy dream? Yes! Because what the fuck do you have to lose? Because you want to just sit the rest of your life and take this shit from your shitty boss and keep complaining?

If that's what you want to do, then this show ain't for you. If that's what you want to do, then keep at it. You know, be a sheep, whatever. That's why I say this show's not for everybody. But play the tape out.
You talk to your wife and you say, listen, this is a crazy idea. And because she's your wife, she used to fucking support you — she goes, honey, this is a crazy dream. Let's play it out to the end.
So then you get the money. You don't know what you're doing. You go to fucking China, you find some weird rubber, and you make this. Long story short, you invent this new rubber band.

That's like ten times stronger than a normal rubber band. Can stretch even wider. And it's like — you replace the old rubber band. And, I don't know, let's say somewhere in the shuffle something gets fucked up, and someone steals your patent or something, and it's all a flop. Are you gonna sit there and go, wow, I had a

dream, I had one silly dream, and I put my whole last decade, years of work, the well-being of me and my family, put myself — because I listened to that fucking idiot with the white hair on his solo podcast — and I put myself out of comfort.

I was perfectly fine. I had grown perfectly numb to my boss and all this shit, and my life was okay. And I took a chance for something better, for a new reality, for some kind of shit where you wake up every morning and go, I can't believe this is my life.

My dad comes home sometimes and kisses me on my fucking mouth and goes, I can't believe I fucking made you. I can't believe I created you. Because every day I wake up in my fucking mansion and I think, goddamn, this life is fucking unbelievable. My dad created me, he raised me well, and I

fucking provided an unreal, surreal life for my family. I took the chance. I fucking went crazy. I gave it all. What are you saving it for? I'm gonna say it over and over again, because you need to ask yourself that. Look at everything — you got it, everything you wanted. If you sit there — and I know a lot of you that watch this show go, I don't want your life,

I like watching you and making fun of you, like you're a fucking silly monkey at the zoo. But this is a small part of my life. The rest of my life — and people go, oh, you seem like, you know, you give really contradicting advice, sometimes I see you say really dark,

negative shit, and this and that — I go, yeah, guess what, I'm depressed as fuck 20% of my life. The other 80% of my life is fucking amazing, and that's a fucking great percentage in my eyes. I love that. Most people, I would say, are 50-50, if that. You know, most people are so unhappy with their life. I

mean, we live in a day and age where we have more comforts — like even poor people have fucking flat-screen TVs, even poor people can afford good food — and we're more miserable than we've ever been, because we're all looking at everyone else saying, I want what he has. Well, you want what the fuck I

have. You want my life, Montblanc, you want my fucking life — then you gotta fucking fight and claw for it. You gotta give up something, you gotta take a chance, you gotta risk something to go get it. So do it. You know, fight for what you want. And when I say take a chance, they'll go, okay, all right,

I'm gonna take a chance. Fucking take a chance like your life depends on it, because guess what — you can be dead tomorrow, and you only got one, you only have one life. That's it. And when you fall down — which you will — most successful self-made millionaires, and the people I'm friends with —

mostly, when it comes to rich people, self-made millionaires — I don't really have a lot of rich friends that were born into it, because they're spoiled pieces of shit. And like my mom says, you know what the problem with spoiling someone is? Once you spoil something, you can't unspoil it. And so if I've learned one thing from all these self-made millionaires,

it's that they fell, and they fell again, and then they fell again — and usually on the third time they wise up, they learned valuable, valuable lessons from the first two, three failures. And that's what I'm saying: secondary gains. If you have a dream and you're young and stupid right now, that's the perfect time — fucking go for it. And you will fall. Some of you will get lucky — very few of

you — will get lucky and just hit and never know what it feels like, the agony of defeat. But those of you who do fall — don't sit there and cry. Turn that. Use the energy, aikido, flip it, use that into something powerful, create secondary gains. Say you spent your life savings — don't say I lost my life savings

on this stupid idea. Say, I spent my life savings on the most valuable lesson, which will help you on the next step. Okay? You have to ask yourself — oh, people, I hate it, because you never know. What is the definition of normal? Oh, that guy's crazy. It's —

it's what I've heard my whole life. That guy's crazy. That guy's crazy. Really? I'm the crazy one? Look at me. Look at me. You look at me and you think I'm crazy? Or, I guess — oh, that guy's unconventional, or — think about it. Think one second, and don't be a fucking sheep for a second,

and think about what is actually crazy. [mock voice] Oh, go to college, oh, do this — it's like you're in a fucking assembly line. Don't you want to live? Do you want to just fucking — I — let me back up. If your focus in life is to procreate and just get people pregnant and just have kids, then

that's your job, just to — that's that. But if I'm talking about someone who wants something more out of life than just being a baby-maker and just multiplying for their own ego, or whatever reasons — [mock voice] I just want a baby, they're so cute, they're so nice to me — guess what, babies grow up to be shitty
teenagers. Babies grow up to be like, fuck you mom and dad. So what really is crazy? I mean, everyone thinks I'm crazy, when I say to myself, I really think I'm a normal person. Why?

Because I enjoy life? Because I attack the things that I want, and I go for it? Does that make me crazy? Like, I was able to go at it so hard, to fucking bend reality around me, to make it what I wanted it to be — as opposed to following you.
I make the rules that you follow. Okay? It's not the other way around, you fucking whining fucking assholes.
You guys fucking get me all fired up. For those of you who didn't hear — I wish I knew the writer — but those of you guys know, I'm in a perpetual state of arrested development.
I have a lot of growing pains. I'm transitioning very slowly. I'm almost 40, I'm 38 years old. But those of you who know me do know that I still buy comic books every Wednesday,

since I was 15 years old. So I read something brilliant. It was Iron Man and the Incredible Hulk — the Incredible Hulk in his Bruce Banner form — sitting at a diner, having a discussion about Tony Stark. Brilliant, brilliant scientist Bruce Banner, brilliant scientist, who invented the gamma bomb, and Tony Stark, who invented the Iron Man suit, as well as a million

other things. Both brilliant. One's a super, super rich playboy, Tony Stark, and Bruce Banner, who's just a vagabond wandering, saying, hey, you wouldn't like me when I'm angry. So obviously Tony Stark, you know, he's done better for himself on a material level, but he's still jealous of Bruce Banner. And so here comes the part where you would
take a chance on yourself. And this is — I don't even know if this is a real thing, since I read it in a fucking comic and I keep quoting it — but it's applied science fiction.

And what that is, is — obviously a time machine doesn't exist. It's impossible, right? But that's the difference between Tony Stark and Bruce Banner. And what I mean by that is: Tony Stark wants to be a genius and create and create.

So the way he does it is, he goes to school, and then he goes to another level of school, and he's a genius so he progresses faster. And so he takes the classes and skills and things he needs, to learn the things that he needs to make.

And that's just the normal way. Applied science fiction is saying — just challenging the impossible. A time machine is impossible, but I'm gonna fucking go ahead and just make it, and figure it out going backwards. And that's a great place to be, if you're young and stupid right now. I'm gonna refer back to

the David Chang episode. You asked him, now, if he would start a restaurant — he said hell no, because guess what, now he knows better, he knows what kind of sacrifice. So when you're young, dumb, and stupid, is the greatest time — when you have all that fucking energy and you don't even know what to do

with it — is applied science fiction. Challenge yourself for shit that's, like, not even in existence. Create realities for yourself that are impossible. [mock whining] Oh, I could never — you think me being a fucking poor fucking chink growing up in Koreatown thought I'd be the highest-paid living artist? Do you think that? Oh, that's just a fucking glitch in the matrix that happened. I fucking planned that for myself.

And I made it happen. Oh, that's because of Sean Parker and Mark Zuckerberg and Facebook. No, motherfucker. I planned this shit. There's a blueprint, and I'm trying to give it to you right now. Applied science fiction. You go backwards. You make impossible goals for yourself, that would be impossible. People will laugh at you when you tell your friends and your family, like, ah,
that's just them being cute. Yeah, it's nice to dream. It's nice to dream. They're never going to do it. You make an impossible goal for yourself, and you do everything. And everyone will tell you —
I've been to every fucking place in the world. When I was 18 years old, I went to the fucking Congo during a fucking Ebola breakout, the biggest AIDS breakout, and the fucking civil war.
'94, '95, around that time. You know what everyone said to me? They were like, don't go to Africa. Don't go to the Congo. This reason and this reason and all these reasons why.
I go, have you ever been to fucking the Congo? No. Most of the world has never been to the Congo. How the fuck are you going to give me advice about a place you've never been to?
So we live in a world that loves to gossip. We live in a world where people love to tell people what to do. And they are speaking of shit they have no fucking idea about.

So when you say, I want to make a time machine — guess what? Someone's gonna say to you, you can't do that. How do you know? Have you ever tried? No. What if a time machine is literally a fucking cardboard box with duct tape on it?

What if that works? You'll know, because you actually tried it — where this fucking hater, this fucking commenting hater, literally just sat there and said, you can't do that. They're haters. They just sit there and they tell you what you can't do.

Have you ever tried? Have you ever been to the Congo? No. How are you gonna speak of things you don't know? Have you ever made a time machine? No. [mock voice] Oh, you just can't. You're just a fucking negative Nancy. Everything's no, I don't know how to do that. And they'll always be like that.

I'm saying: try. And when I say try harder and all that kind of shit, work harder — it's a joke. Because you can't try harder. You just do it. Like fucking Yoda said, like Charles Bukowski said — don't try to do something, because then you're just setting yourself up to fail.
Just do it. No fucking retreat, no surrender, no exceptions. Don't go, I'm going to wake up tomorrow and try to accomplish this goal. You will do it, at all costs, no matter what.

That level of dedication. You think Ninja and Yolandi and Die Antwoord, living in a fucking slum in fucking Africa, thought they were going to be international rap superstars? They fucking wanted it so bad that they turned their dream into a reality.
If it doesn't work out for you, try and try again. Try harder, and don't even try — just make it happen. There's no other option. Failure is not an option. Just fucking do it.

Ah. Alright. You guys, I swear to God, you guys get me so fucking worked up, I don't even know who I'm talking to right now. Am I talking to the 15-year-old version of myself? When I try to visualize who the fuck I'm talking to right now — it's so crazy, but the same things keep coming up. And as a person who's 38

years old with an extreme amount of wealth — and people ask me all kinds of shit — you guys have heard me on the show, I put myself in a perpetual state of uncomfortableness. Self-imposed prisons, situations where I don't let myself have sex for months. And through these things, I find creativity. I know that's not the answer for everyone, but these are the things that
